My co-founders and I starte...
items.content:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.

The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.

This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission.

items.content:
Whoa, great and even excessive Marin Mochi (535B-A23B) checkpoint drop (in a good way!)

Comes with great tech report btw with insights into why / how components were picked (for training stability and GPU throughput).

Short fact sheet:

1) Latent MoE with an extra RMSNorm on the latent that made latent MoE actually work (better)

2) Classic 3:1 sliding-window/global gated GQA, partial RoPE (local) and NoPE (global)

3) Adding short convolutions on keys, attention output, and MoE output

4) Exclusive self-attention (XSA) -- I guess the end-of-the year architecture roundup this year won't be boring 😅

items.title: Sharing new research on self-improving skills in Perplexity Computer. Brain, which already maintains...
items.content: Sharing new research on self-improving skills in Perplexity Computer. Brain, which already maintains a knowledge wiki about your work, now also writes and updates agent skills for you based on your past sessions. An improvement agent reads the full session trajectories (tool calls, reasoning, results), finds recurring patterns, and only proposes a new skill or an update when there’s enough evidence. Built-in skills that every user gets go through paired replay on failure scenarios and engineer review before any change goes live. In an 8-week randomized test on production traffic, 72.9% of users got at least one new personal skill vs 6.5% who added one manually. Tool call failures dropped 11% and dissatisfied threads dropped 7.6%, with no measurable change in cost or latency.

items.title: NEW: Google DeepMind researcher Tim Genewein published an essay on how AI could get from human-level...
items.content:
NEW: Google DeepMind researcher Tim Genewein published an essay on how AI could get from human-level (AGI) to superintelligence (ASI).

Genewein says the count of today's AI agents the world can run might grow more than 1,000x by 2030 and pass a billion times within a decade.

Beyond just numbers, he names four routes: bigger models trained on more data, new ways of building AI, large groups of agents working together, and AI that improves the next generation of AI.

He also says the routes build on each other, and if one stalls, competition will likely push work onto the others.

items.title: In September, we described a few ways we're improving the accuracy and relevance of our AI progress ...
items.content:
In September, we described a few ways we're improving the accuracy and relevance of our AI progress forecasts. In the most recent wave from our Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP), we've experimented with a few potential improvements, including:

• Adding more questions with short-term resolutions to enable faster identification of more accurate forecasters
• Improving the information we give to forecasters as they're forecasting
• Adding new forecasters with track records of accuracy
• Separating out forecasts from a subgroup of experts who expect fast AI progress
• Repeating questions from earlier waves to understand how forecasters' views change over time

Read on for initial results from these experiments 🧵

Abundant's @quasicoh explains what existing RSI benc...
items.content:
"RSI has to be about Claude improving Claude."

Abundant's @quasicoh explains what existing RSI benchmarks are getting wrong:

"In order to have true RSI, it needs to have recursion. You need an LLM to improve an LLM so that you can have a recursive loop."

"If you have Claude improve Waymo, there's no way for Waymo to improve Claude."

"We were looking at other benchmarks that were labeled as RSI, but we were a little bit disappointed in them because they were mostly focused on whether AI can improve other types of AI."
@abundant_labs

items.title: Building a great benchmark is challenging, building a perfect benchmark is near impossible. This esp...
items.content:
Building a great benchmark is challenging, building a perfect benchmark is near impossible. This especially holds true in the world of document parsing.

I wrote a blog post that details the core design criteria needed for a document parsing benchmark, and the historical attempts to get there - from those based on static deterministic metrics to LLM as a judge approaches.

Building a “great” benchmark requires at least the following:
1. Representative data
2. Granularity
3. Quantifiable
4. Repeatable
5. Controllable
6. Aligned with human judgment

Existing benchmarks based on deterministic metrics are oftentimes granular/repeatable, but not controllable or aligned with human judgment. Those based on LLM as a judge are not granular, quantifiable, repeatable, and can obscure how human judgment is encoded.

Last week we launched ParseBench-2 in an attempt to tackle all of these dimensions. It contains a taxonomy of metrics across 6 dimensions (tables, charts, layout, formatting, text, and forms) that precisely measure document parsing failures and quantifies their impact. items.content_html:
Building a great benchmark is challenging, building a perfect benchmark is near impossible. This especially holds true in the world of document parsing.

I wrote a blog post that details the core design criteria needed for a document parsing benchmark, and the historical attempts to get there - from those based on static deterministic metrics to LLM as a judge approaches.

Building a “great” benchmark requires at least the following:

1. Representative data

2. Granularity

3. Quantifiable

4. Repeatable

5. Controllable

6. Aligned with human judgment

Existing benchmarks based on deterministic metrics are oftentimes granular/repeatable, but not controllable or aligned with human judgment. Those based on LLM as a judge are not granular, quantifiable, repeatable, and can obscure how human judgment is encoded.

Last week we launched ParseBench-2 in an attempt to tackle all of these dimensions. It contains a taxonomy of metrics across 6 dimensions (tables, charts, layout, formatting, text, and forms) that precisely measure document parsing failures and quantifies their impact. It’s certainly not perfect, but does make an honest attempt towards advancing every design criteria. It’s also designed to be customizable by the user (see our metric lab!)

We’re rapidly shipping new iterations of this benchmark to improve annotations, metric quality, and customizability. If you do check it out, would love to hear your thoughts.

Blog: https://t.co/NAchVsDfVC

ParseBench-2: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX

items.content:
Graph-aware search beats semantic search every day of the week and twice on Sunday.

I spent all night putting together an example to show you how cool graph retrieval is.

1. You store facts as persistent memory records.

2. You connect records with links labeled with their relationships. For example, "supersedes," "supports," or "contradicts".

3. You then use these links to retrieve the proper records.

If you need to store information with relationships between facts, you want to look into this.

Oracle AI Agent Memory 26.8 implements graph-aware search.

Here is a blog post explaining how Graph-aware search works in Oracle:

https://t.co/OhGOuR6aZG

Thanks to the @OracleDevs team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Lab-grown chicken is now being served at restaurants across California after UPSIDE Foods announced a major breakthrough in production scale and cost.

• UPSIDE Chicken is now available at 8 California restaurants, including San Francisco's Epic Steak and Waterbar, as well as Stanford University dining facilities

• Unlike plant-based meat, cultivated chicken is grown from real chicken cells in bioreactors. UPSIDE's new product combines these cells with ingredients like soy protein, pea fiber, and olive oil

• UPSIDE says it has scaled production 10,000-fold and can now produce over 1 million pounds annually using 20,000-liter tanks

• The company says production costs have fallen more than 10-fold, with restaurant dishes now selling for $12–$19, comparable to premium conventional chicken dishes

• UPSIDE first received regulatory clearance in 2023, but high production costs limited its availability. The new rollout marks its first broad commercial launch

@sophiadew: "Lab-grown meat had a lot of hype a decade ago, but the cost of producing it held the industry back. Now we're starting to see that change."

items.content:
What happens next with cyber outages?

"I think it's only gonna get worse."

"We generate code now at 10x the velocity. We don't have 10x more engineers to run these systems."

"And on top of that, because of all the security vulnerabilities, we are patching these systems now at 10x, 50x the speed than before."

"Unless AI adoption for running production software and solving these problems gets on par with coding and security, we cannot keep up."

"The answer to all of this is AI that can be on the defense, that can help us maintain, patch, and run these systems at the same velocity that we find security vulnerabilities or make changes with AI."

From Industry News with @sophiadew and @resolveai CEO @spirosx

items.title:
"Hey Grok, why is this important and explain it in language a nine-year-old can understand."

"Sure,...
items.content:
"Hey Grok, why is this important and explain it in language a nine-year-old can understand."

"Sure, here you go:"

"Imagine you have a big box of different toys — cars, animals, blocks — and a robot friend who is trying to learn what each one is by looking at them and guessing what they will do next. That robot is a bit like the AI this post is talking about (called JEPA).

The problem is that sometimes the robot gets lazy. After a little while it starts thinking *every* toy is basically the same. Then it can’t tell them apart anymore and stops learning anything useful. Scientists call this “collapse.” It happens a lot with this kind of AI, so training either fails or takes forever.

SADL is a new, simple rule the researchers added. It keeps the robot noticing the differences between toys so it never gets stuck. In their tests the collapse problem went from happening half the time (or more) to never happening. The robot also learned much faster — sometimes in one try what used to take ten tries — and got better at understanding pictures and controlling things.

That’s important because if AI can learn about the real world more reliably and quickly (without getting confused or giving up), it can help with things like smarter robots, better games, or machines that understand what’s happening around them — all without needing someone to label every single example.

"I believe Anthropic had a blog post about how, on some of their models, they reduced their capabilities for RSI-type tasks."

"We observed a few cases where it was like safety, something was flagged.

"Basically, we had no refusals on our benchmark. There were cases where the safety guardrail was blocking something, but then the agent just retried, and then it was fine."

"The refusals did occur, but they didn't block the agents from completing their tasks. So the numbers don't need any adjustment for that."

We asked updated versions of two questions that we asked LEAP panelists in earlier waves:

• Whether AI will help solve another Millennium Prize Problem (originally asked in summer 2025)
• The combined annualized revenue run rate of Anthropic and OpenAI (originally asked in summer 2026)

LEAP forecasters have majorly updated toward more AI progress. In mid-2025, the median expert thought there was only a 20% chance that AI would help solve a Millennium Prize Problem by the end of 2030.

Now the median expert thinks there is an 80% chance that at least one additional Millennium Prize Problem will be solved by AI by 2030. The median expert also thinks there is now a 45% chance that AI helps solve an additional three or more Millennium Prize Problems (not counting Navier–Stokes) by the end of 2030, and an 80% chance by the end of 2040.

Superforecasters and AI risk experts also updated their predictions of frontier labs' combined revenue at the end of 2026 and 2030 by roughly 2x compared with their earlier forecasts.

items.title:
Hot take: The people calling for Jensen to be brought back are hurting NVIDIA at this point.

He isn...
items.content:
Hot take: The people calling for Jensen to be brought back are hurting NVIDIA at this point.

He isn't coming back. I don't believe there are enough shareholders coming to vote to fire the board and extend this shit show.

So where does this lead us? 

A world of pain. 

As if the last week or two hasn't been enough.

Get ready for more pain.

But at some point capitulation will happen. Everyone will see that bringing back Jensen won't happen.

Then what?

Investors should, instead, be looking at the depth of leadership in this company. Looking at its strengths and asking themselves "what kind of leader do we want to see put in place?" Who can come in and get everyone to see a new vision for NVIDIA?

Is there a leader on the field who can keep NVIDIA's strengths and minimize its weaknesses.

I found one yesterday.

Ferrari's CEO, Benedetto Vigna, who spoke about the role of innovation at the Slush Conference yesterday. Which was quite excellent, by the way.

He knows a lot more about that, and running a company that has a leadership position, than anyone else I can see.

You might knock him about how he launched Ferrari's electric vehicle, which is sold out now, by the way, and paves the path for more innovation at @Ferrari.

Convince him to join as CEO of NVIDIA. That would get the world to see NVIDIA has a leader who can continue its innovation and leadership role.

This "bring Jensen back" movement just isn't gonna lead us to a good place. 

As much as I believe he was wrongfully, or, at minimum, awfully, fired, that ship has sailed and it's time to find a new leader who can step in and get NVIDIA headed in a new direction.

This "bring Jensen back" kind of belief just will increase NVIDIA's pain and extend it for years. 

Time for new, bold, leadership to take NVIDIA out of the morass it is in.

We defined a new subset of LEAP experts based on their expectations of AI progress. This "fast AI progress" group gave the following forecasts in earlier waves:

• A combined probability of more than 50% that AI reaches level 9 or 10 on the Technological Richter Scale by 2040
• A probability of at least 90% that, by 2100, more than half of LEAP panelists will agree that AGI exists
• A median forecast of 2040 or earlier for when AGI arrives

In this wave, approximately 40 out of 276 experts and AI risk experts met these criteria.

This group of "fast AI progress" experts gave broadly similar forecasts for short-term questions resolving in 2026 to those of other experts. However, for questions with resolution dates beyond 2026, the forecasts from the "fast AI progress" group diverged from other experts.

One implication of this is that these short-term resolving questions will not substantially differentiate these groups’ medians in terms of accuracy. They may still be useful, though, in differentiating individuals’ accuracy.

items.title: Abundant's @quasicoh and Jesse Hu argue that banning RSI could hinder AI alignment, since the same t...
items.content:
Abundant's @quasicoh and Jesse Hu argue that banning RSI could hinder AI alignment, since the same techniques that make AI more capable can also make it safer:

Jesse: "We look at model training as a tool in a toolbox that a lot of people can use. In medicine, you might need custom pathology, oncology models.

"In material science or synthetic biology, you need to be able to train models specific to that use case. RSI in the weaker sense could be one of those things."

"What we're studying is more on the stronger side, where the model's working on optimizers and other things that are part of the frontier LLM coding agent stack. But those things also generalize to the rest of the applications. It’s hard to decouple those two."

Kevin: "In a lot of this discourse, people tend to suggest that they're vectors pointing in opposite directions, and maybe they cancel each other out. I would describe them as orthogonal vectors.

"Working on alignment doesn't hurt capabilities, and working on capabilities doesn't hurt alignment."

Jesse: "We're encouraging the model to be better at data mixes, data synthesis, post-training techniques, and these are the same techniques we need to utilize in alignment as well."

"If we can point those abilities in the right vector, that's a way for models to also be part of the alignment story."

Kevin: "We view alignment as a part of capabilities. Alignment is a part of RSI. So RSI can also accelerate alignment."
@abundant_labs @Madisonkanna

From Ferry Health co-founder @MMehta17: "There's...
items.content:
How does Anthropic IPO affect healthcare startups?

From Ferry Health co-founder @MMehta17: "There's no better time to have started a company around this mission."

"There's so much money going into these capabilities."

"We're the beneficiaries of all this amazing technology, aimed at a trillion-dollar problem that is ultimately one of the great millennium questions of the American society."

"We think of ourselves working alongside the labs, not competitive. The messiness of navigating healthcare... in some ways is not really an expertise problem, it's really a dedicated solution problem."

"It's not like a model that gets 10x better overnight just instantly zaps that problem. It's a really complicated thing around how you think about the supply of providers and working with them to get the best patients."

"I don't think of that as a model problem. I think of that as a coordination problem... It's not just a pure compute and inference type of thing."

From Industry News with @sophiadew

items.content:
How should companies prepare for cyber outages?

"My advice to IT, security leaders and CEOs is that these are very hard domains for building on your own."

"You should find the best companies and models to collaborate with."

"I would say probably you have to collaborate with a different company in coding, a different company in security, reliability, etc. I don't think there's anybody who can do all of that."

"I don't believe the labs by themselves can solve this problem either. They are developing great models, but the last mile complexity in delivering a system reliably and securely is very, very difficult. So you need specialization."

From Industry News with @sophiadew and @resolveai CEO @spirosx

𝗦𝗲𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀' 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

We experimented...
items.content:
𝗦𝗲𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀' 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

We experimented with showing some LEAP respondents the running median forecast for each question from respondents who had already submitted their forecasts. Respondents who were randomly selected into this group (50% of superforecasters and experts) also received a mid-wave email summarizing rationales from other forecasters.

We didn't observe any meaningful differences in the median forecast between participants who saw the running median and those who did not. Exposure to the running median also didn't change the spread of respondents' forecasts.

In this wave, all participants were shown LLM-generated forecasts after submitting their initial forecast on each question. It is possible that respondents in both groups anchored to the LLM forecast and that this effect washed out any potential effects of shared aggregates. In Wave 14, we're randomizing who sees the LLM forecasts to partially test this hypothesis.

items.reasoning: Careful experimental methodology with a genuinely interesting hypothesis about LLM forecasts anchoring human forecasters; low engagement but original and rigorous.
items.summary_html: Research_FRI reports a randomized experiment showing exposure to running median forecasts did not change respondents' predictions, and outlines a Wave 14 design to test anchoring on LLM-generated forecasts.
items.content_html:
𝗦𝗲𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀' 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

We experimented with showing some LEAP respondents the running median forecast for each question from respondents who had already submitted their forecasts. Respondents who were randomly selected into this group (50% of superforecasters and experts) also received a mid-wave email summarizing rationales from other forecasters.

We didn't observe any meaningful differences in the median forecast between participants who saw the running median and those who did not. Exposure to the running median also didn't change the spread of respondents' forecasts.

In this wave, all participants were shown LLM-generated forecasts after submitting their initial forecast on each question. It is possible that respondents in both groups anchored to the LLM forecast and that this effect washed out any potential effects of shared aggregates. In Wave 14, we're randomizing who sees the LLM forecasts to partially test this hypothesis.

Applied Probability is a first textbook in probability, designed for readers with a moderate level of mathematical sophistication.

It builds a precise model of uncertainty from outcomes and events, using set theory to describe event combinations and probability measures to assign likelihoods.

The book presents probability as a framework for representing practical uncertainty, with examples tied to engineering, science, management, reliability, and statistical analysis.

items.title: Siri is an embarrassment. Everyone is releasing assistants that do 10x more and better than Apple's ...
items.content:
Siri is an embarrassment. Everyone is releasing assistants that do 10x more and better than Apple's own.

@meetJdoe is a new assistant you can install on your Mac and your iPhone. You can join the beta using this link: https://t.co/Go6SyE1DaY

It's pretty straightforward:

1. Give it access to context: notes, images, voice recordings, or even your Mac's screen.

2. J.Doe will use that context to suggest actions using decision cards. Each card includes supporting information so you can review the suggestion.

3. The more you use it, the better it gets. You can also inspect everything it knows about you in the app.

4. Obviously, J.Doe can also execute tasks for you if you approve them.

Something I love:

The agent can even pass work to Codex or Claude Code on your computer! They are also planning to launch their own hardware in 2027.

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

items.title: AI-generated quizzes like those automatically built for users on ChapterPal are a great way to test ...
items.content:
AI-generated quizzes like those automatically built for users on ChapterPal are a great way to test your understanding of complex material.

It might sound counterintuitive, but even when the quiz sometimes asks the wrong question or marks the wrong option as correct, this gets the user thinking about why this happened and looking to justify their correct answer, which was marked as wrong. This additional investigation results in better learning and retention.

When there are 5 or more answer options, especially when the user should choose more than one option, it is extremely unlikely that an attentive user will conclude that a wrong answer is correct, choose it, and happen to choose the exact wrong answer that the AI also thought was correct. This is no more likely than with human-built quizzes.
items.author: @burkov
items.summary: Andriy Burkov argues that AI-generated quizzes on ChapterPal are effective for learning even when they contain errors, because users investigate discrepancies between their answers and the marked-correct ones, deepening retention. He reasons that with 5+ answer options the chance an attentive user coincidentally picks the same wrong option as the AI is no higher than with human-written quizzes.
items.reasoning: Burkov is a recognized ML author, and the post offers a somewhat original argument about error-tolerant AI tutoring, but it is promotional for his own product with low engagement (12 likes, 1406 views).

@Joe_Anandarajah He isn't coming back. Get that through your head: he is not coming back.

So I don'...
items.content:
@Joe_Anandarajah He isn't coming back. Get that through your head: he is not coming back.

So I don't care about the stock. I care about finding a leader who can bring this company into the future: somebody who understands how to run big companies, someone who understands innovation, someone who is a winner, and someone who can get employees to listen and work together to fix all the problems that are going to come up over the next couple of quarters.

I think you're reading the CFO, now interim CEO, very poorly. She's just there to give the company time to breathe and find a new leader, and she's done a competent job so far. She was thrown into the job very quickly, without any planning, without anybody saying, "Hey, she's the one." She knows her role well, and people who know her say she's very capable. I think throwing rocks at her right now is going to lead you to a bad place.

This company is not going away. And yeah, I'm an investor: I'm staying long. I see this company going on and having a great future, but it does have a leadership problem at the moment because everybody is yelling and screaming and throwing bananas at the stage.

Well, you have to find a leader who can get everybody to calm down and pull in one direction. That's what we should be looking at. Jensen's not coming back. It's time to find a new leader and new leadership.

I care about finding a leader who can bring this company into the future: somebody who understands how to run big companies, someone who understands innovation, someone who is a winner, and someone who can get employees to listen and work together to fix all the problems that are going to come up over the next couple of quarters.

I think you're reading the CFO, now interim CEO, very poorly. She's just there to give the company time to breathe and find a new leader, and she's done a competent job so far. She was thrown into the job very quickly, without any planning, without anybody saying, "Hey, she's the one." She knows her role well, and people who know her say she's very capable. I think throwing rocks at her right now is going to lead you to a bad place.

This company is not going away. And yeah, I'm an investor: I'm staying long. I see this company going on and having a great future, but it does have a leadership problem at the moment because everybody is yelling and screaming and throwing bananas at the stage.

Well, you have to find a leader who can get everybody to calm down and pull in one direction. That's what we should be looking at. Jensen's not coming back. It's time to find a new leader and new leadership.

An operatin...
items.content:
A free online book: Operating System Fundamentals by Umar Khokhar and Binh Tran (2023).

An operating system is the software layer that connects users and applications with computer hardware, allocates shared resources, and provides a platform for programs to run.

The book develops this view from basic computer organization and OS goals into the mechanisms that make systems work, then applies those ideas to contemporary operating systems and cloud computing. 

The book is suited to readers seeking a structured introduction to operating-system concepts, including the terminology and models used to reason about system behavior.

items.summary_html: Scoble tells critics to accept Jensen's departure, arguing NVIDIA's leadership depth means the company is not going away and proposing the search for a credible successor rather than calls to bring Jensen back.
items.content_html:
@mr_sunglow Get over it: Jensen's gone, and he's not coming back. Now you have to find a leader who can take over Nvidia and do a credible job.

If you think this company is done, you're just not rational, or maybe you just don't understand the company. This company has such depth of leadership and talent that even if a third of them left, they would still have more than even Anthropic has. So this company is not going away.

The only question in my mind is: who's going to be the leader, and does that leader have credibility to lead? The head of Ferrari does, and I'm sure there's quite a list of others out there who could. We should be talking about that rather than this "bring Jensen back" bullshit, because he ain't coming back.

items.title: @rayvahey If you give a correct answer but the quiz tells you that it's wrong, you don't just accept...
items.content: @rayvahey If you give a correct answer but the quiz tells you that it's wrong, you don't just accept it. You try to figure out why you came to this "wrong" conclusion. And then you figure out that you weren't wrong. This investigation is the most effective way of learning. If you just accept the wrong answer and move on, you don't learn properly. It's up to the learner to decide whether they want to learn or just finish reading.
items.author: @burkov
